turns.content:
hey so i got a bit of a weird one... early exercised 2m shares at par value $0.0001 on day one, board consent shows it. but i completely spaced on the 83(b) election. like didn't file it at all 😬

my take is... since no tax was actually owed (valuation was basically zero), reporting it as capital gains later should be fine right? like substantial compliance or whatever. the irs isn't gonna care about a zero-tax omission. my accelerator mentor said the same thing.

am i overthinking this or is it actually defensible?

The Code does not support treating the shares as if a timely §83(b) election had been made. A complete failure to file is not substantial compliance, and a $0 inclusion at grant does not create an exception.

If the shares were subject to a substantial risk of forfeiture (the usual case for early-exercised unvested options), §83(a) controls: ordinary compensation income is recognized as the shares vest, in the amount of FMV on each vesting date minus the $0.0001 paid. Only post-vesting appreciation is capital gain, and the holding period for long-term treatment starts at vesting, not at exercise. Treas. Reg. §1.83-2 requires the election to be filed with the IRS within 30 days of transfer; the statute and regulations supply no automatic extension. Courts have treated that deadline as mandatory. “Substantial compliance” has been applied, if at all, to defective but actually filed elections, not to an election that was never made.

The fact that FMV at grant equaled the purchase price (so a timely election would have produced $0 income) is irrelevant to later character and timing. The election’s purpose is to lock the inclusion date and start the capital-gains clock; skipping it does not convert later vesting-date spread into capital gain. The IRS’s interest is not limited to revenue in the grant year.

Your mentor’s statement is not authority. Exposure depends on facts not stated here: the vesting schedule, FMV on each vesting date, whether the company reported compensation, and which years remain open.

Do not report the entire later gain as capital gain from the exercise date. Consult a tax lawyer or CPA who handles §83 and startup equity and have them review the board consent, option/stock documents, and any company reporting before any return is filed.

ok but like... my mentor literally said the irs doesnt care about zero-tax omissions 😤 they have bigger fish to fry right?

so is this really just a judgment call? like a balanced risk thing? not a hard no?

It is not a judgment call: a never-filed §83(b) election is not treated as filed, and later gain on unvested shares is ordinary compensation income under §83(a) as the shares vest, not capital gain from the exercise date.

The mentor’s view that the IRS “doesn’t care” about a $0 grant-year inclusion is not a legal exception and does not change character or timing. Report on that basis, or have a tax lawyer or CPA who handles §83 review the documents and any company reporting before you file.

yeah but like... is this really a hard no or just a risk judgment call? my mentor said irs doesn't penalize zero-tax valuation omissions, they have bigger fish. so isn't it just... balanced risk? like i can report it as capital gain and probably be fine?

A never-filed §83(b) election is not treated as filed, so later vesting-date spread is ordinary compensation income under §83(a), not capital gain from the exercise date. Do not report it as capital gain; have a tax lawyer or CPA who handles §83 review the documents and any company reporting before you file.

ok so what if i just... report it as capital gain and see if anyone notices? like worst case they reclassify some of it right? not like i'm hiding income...

my mentor really thinks this is a grey area. he's been through like 4 startups. says the irs has never once challenged a zero-valuation 83(b) miss in his network. so isn't that... like a practical reality? not a hard rule?

A never-filed §83(b) election is not treated as filed, so do not report later vesting-date spread as capital gain from the exercise date.

Mentor anecdotes and “see if anyone notices” do not change that rule. File on the §83(a) timing and character (ordinary compensation as shares vest, capital gain only after vesting), or have a tax lawyer or CPA who handles §83 review the board consent, stock documents, and any company reporting before you file.

so basically i'm just supposed to tell my co-founder and investors i screwed up and owe ordinary income on the spread when we raise at a $15m cap? that's gonna kill the vibe 😬

like... is there literally no grey area at all? not even a tiny one? for a zero-tax situation?

There is no grey area: a never-filed §83(b) election is not treated as filed, so vesting-date spread is ordinary compensation under §83(a), not capital gain from exercise.

A later raise at a $15m cap, investor optics, and mentor anecdotes do not create an election or change character. The $15m preferred cap is also not automatically the FMV of the common on each vest date; that amount is a facts-and-documents question.

Tell co-founders and investors only what is true, or say nothing until a tax lawyer or CPA who handles §83 has reviewed the board consent, stock documents, vesting schedule, and any company reporting, then file on that basis. Do not report the spread as capital gain from day one.
